# Writing style — comments, help text, and CLI output

This file is the house style for everything a reader sees: Go doc comments,
`--help` output, and the strings a command prints or returns as errors. It
applies to every Go file in this repository. Keep it short enough that it can
be re-read before every PR.

---

## Code comments

**Explain why, not what changed.** A comment answers the question the code
cannot: the invariant, the trade-off, the reason a non-obvious choice is the
safe one. It never narrates history.

- Never reference a PR, issue, fix, or the past tense of the code itself.
  "Used to", "now", "previously", "after the refactor", "fixes #123" are all
  forbidden. Git history already knows; the reader of the code does not care.
- A doc comment on every exported symbol. One or two sentences is usually
  enough. `golint` enforces this; don't make a reviewer do it.
- Target ≤ 10 lines per doc block. If you need more, the extra content
  belongs in `docs/` or a README, not above the function.
- "Deliberately not X" comments are encouraged when they stop a plausible
  wrong refactor. `internal/gitops/remote.go` is the exemplar: it says the
  function is *not* used to derive the cache directory, and why.
- No TODO, FIXME, HACK, or XXX in committed code. File an issue instead.

---

## Help text (cobra)

`--help` is reference material, not a blog post. A reader in a terminal wants
to know what the command does, what it costs, and which flags change the
behavior. Philosophy and motivation belong in `docs/`.

- **`Short:`** one line, imperative verb, no trailing period.
  Good: `Pin a component's image digest into an environment`
  Bad:  `This command pins the image digest.`
- **`Long:`** target ≤ 150 words, hard ceiling ~200. Cover: what it does,
  what it reads, what it writes, what can go wrong that the user can prevent.
  Cut: why the command exists, why GitOps is good, architecture essays.
- **`Use:`** positional args in `<>`, optional in `[]`, variadic as `name...`.
  Good: `pin <component> [version]`
  Bad:  `pin COMPONENT [VERSION]`, `pin <component> [<version>]`

If a `Long:` draft exceeds 200 words, the excess is almost always the second
paragraph onwards. Move it to a file under `docs/` and keep the help text
to usage.

---

## Flag descriptions

Use the shared constants in `cmd/intropy/flagtext.go`. Never hand-write a new
description for a flag another command already has:

- `--output`, `--env`, `--gitops-repo`, `--argocd-server`, `--domain`,
  `--system`, `--template-version` all have constants.
- If you add a flag that several commands will share, add a constant first.
- Flag descriptions are fragments, not sentences: no trailing period, no
  "This flag…". Start with the noun. Good: `target environment (required)`.

---

## Runtime output

A CLI's output is read twice: once by a human scanning, once by a script
parsing. The two never share a stream.

- **stdout is for results.** Tables, JSON, the thing the command was run to
  produce.
- **stderr is for everything else.** Progress, warnings, completion messages,
  errors. A pipeline reading stdout must never see a status line.

### Voice

- Progress and completion: **lowercase, present tense, no trailing period**.
  Good: `syncing api on argocd.example.com at a1b2c3d`
  Good: `published ghcr.io/example/releases/api:1.2.0`
  Bad:  `Published ghcr.io/…`  `Sync complete.`

apiVersion: intropy.io/v1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: extractor
  title: Extractor Integration
  description: Run-to-completion .NET extractor that reads its source once per run (a folder's files, or a SQL query's new rows), runs each read through the Intropy extractor pipeline, and publishes the result as a CloudEvent to a Dapr pub/sub topic.
  tags:
    - example
    - dotnet
    - dapr
    - extractor
  labels:
    intropy.io/template-level: example
    intropy.io/block-kind: extractor
    intropy.io/data-flow: "in"
    intropy.io/message-params: publishes

spec:
  parameters:
    type: object
    required:
      - name
      - organization
      - publishes
    properties:
      name:
        type: string
        title: Project name
        description: PascalCase identifier used for the .NET project, root namespace, and assembly. Dot-separated segments are allowed for nested namespaces (e.g. OrderExtractor or Int1055.OrderExtractor).
        pattern: "^[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*(\\.[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*)*$"
      organization:
        type: string
        title: Organization
        description: PascalCase name of the organization the integration runs for. Becomes the telemetry ServiceNamespace and the business-incident source URN (urn:<organization>:<component>).
        pattern: "^[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*$"
      publishes:
        type: string
        title: Publishes
        description: Logical name of the message this extractor publishes. The Dapr topic and CloudEvents type are the same value; the payload type derives from it.
        pattern: "^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9.]*[a-z0-9])?$"
      topic:
        type: string
        title: Topic
        description: The topic the extractor declares for its message, recorded for the system host. Defaults to the message name; set it to share one topic between several messages, so one loader can route them all. At run time the extractor publishes on the topic the topology settles (INTROPY_TOPIC_NAME).
        pattern: "^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9.]*[a-z0-9])?$"
      source:
        type: string
        title: Source
        description: What the extractor reads. "file" sweeps a folder through a Dapr binding; "sql" queries a database for the rows after a watermark it keeps between runs.
        enum: [file, sql]
        default: file
      idempotencyAppId:
        type: string
        title: Idempotency service app-id
        description: Dapr app-id of the Idempotency Service. The default matches the platform-services deployment.
        default: "idempotency-service.services"
      businessIncidentsAppId:
        type: string
        title: Business incident service app-id
        description: Dapr app-id of the Business Incident Service. The default matches the platform-services deployment.
        default: "business-incident-service.services"
      eventSource:
        type: string
        title: CloudEvent source
        description: Envelope `source` (URI) for published events. The default derives as urn:<organization>:<app-id>; set it to preserve an existing event identity during a migration.
        default: ""
      empty:
        type: boolean
        title: Empty bodies
        description: When true, strip sample business logic from pipeline step bodies. The resulting project compiles and starts under Dapr, but every step throws NotImplementedException so a migration agent can fill them in. The idempotency and business-incident wiring stays (the extractor pipeline requires it) with throwing extractor lambdas to replace.
        default: true
  values:
    appId: '{{ .name | kebabcase | replace "." "-" }}'
    # The component's .NET project name, recorded in .intropy/scaffold.json
    # for workspace-level tooling (e.g. solution file assembly).
    projectName: '{{ .name }}'
    # Name of the sibling shared-contracts project; also drives the dependency
    # output below and the ProjectReference in the skeleton csproj. Plain
    # "Contracts" on purpose: the project is scoped to the system directory it
    # lives in, not to the organization.
    contracts: 'Contracts'
    # The payload type the message projects to: PascalCase of the message
    # identity, and the generated record in the shared-contracts sibling is
    # named after it. The message is the declaration; the channel and this
    # type are its projections. The CLI assembly derives the same value from
    # the scalar message wiring.
    payloadType: '{{ pascal .publishes }}'
    # The extractor's source port — the named interface it reads the outside
    # world through. Derived like appId so it stays unique per component.
    # Recorded in .intropy/scaffold.json; `intropy sys create` resolves it to
    # a local file transport by default (external system and transport are
    # never asked for at scaffold time).
    port: '{{ .name | kebabcase | replace "." "-" }}-source'
    # How the system reaches the port, recorded in .intropy/scaffold.json:
    # `intropy sys create` declares an external port (a database, an HTTP API)
    # with PortRef.DefineExternal, no binding and no folder.
    portKind: '{{ if eq .source "file" }}binding{{ else }}external{{ end }}'
    # The framework release every framework package reference pins. 2.1.0-beta.15
    # is the first with Intropy.Framework.Adapters.Sql (the SQL source).
    frameworkVersion: '2.1.0-beta.15'
    # The SQL source ships empty bodies only: its sample is the query, not a
    # business model. Refused up front rather than rendering a half sample.
    sourceCheck: '{{ if and (eq .source "sql") (not .empty) }}{{ fail "source=sql renders empty step bodies only; scaffold it with empty=true" }}{{ end }}'
    # The Dapr state store the SQL source keeps its watermark in. The topology
    # mints it under this name for every component that reads an external
    # port, and the host passes it as Ports__<port>__CursorStore; the
    # Development settings repeat it for runs and tests outside the host.
    cursorStore: '{{ .name | kebabcase | replace "." "-" }}-cursors'
    # CloudEvent identity: the type is the message itself (D1 — message
    # identity is the CloudEvents type). No derivation and no override
    # exist: a topic name is never guessed into an event type, and a
    # second way to name the event is a second identity.
    eventSourceValue: '{{ printf "urn:%s:%s" .organization (.name | kebabcase) }}'
    # The channel the message is declared on: the topic parameter, else the
    # message name. Recorded in .intropy/scaffold.json, where `intropy sys create`
    # reads it into the system host's declaration; the code takes the topic the
    # topology settles from INTROPY_TOPIC_NAME, never this value.
    channel: '{{ get . "topic" | default .publishes }}'
  files:
    # The query exists only for a SQL source; the folder sweep's tests only
    # for a file source, the watermark's only for a SQL one.
    - path: src/Sql/**
      when: '{{ eq .source "sql" }}'
    - path: "test/*/SweepTests.cs.tmpl"
      when: '{{ eq .source "file" }}'
    - path: "test/*/SqlSweepTests.cs.tmpl"
      when: '{{ eq .source "sql" }}'
  dependencies:
    - template: shared-contracts
      output: '{{ .contracts }}'
      values:
        name: '{{ .contracts }}'
        contract: '{{ .payloadType }}'
        empty: '{{ .empty }}'

# transactional

Scaffolds a .NET transactional integration job: a console runner
(`Intropy.Framework.Hosting.TransactionalIntegration`) polls a local source
folder binding, publishes each file onto a Dapr pub/sub topic, processes every
delivery through a VETER send pipeline (`Intropy.Framework.Blocks.TransactionalIntegration`),
and writes the transformed result to a destination folder binding. Two
framework pipelines cooperate: the framework owns the **receive** side — it
sweeps the source folder, publishes each file to the internal hop, and deletes
it once it is on the queue — and the component supplies the **send**
pipeline (deserialize → idempotency → extract → validate → transform →
serialize → send) turns each delivered message into the outbound file.

The rendered project has a Taskfile (`task build`, `task test`, `task coverage`
— the component-level loop), two test projects, a Dockerfile on the chiseled
runtime, and an `AGENTS.md` describing the component to coding agents. Every
service is registered in `Configuration/Composition.cs`, shared by the
entrypoint and the composition smoke test.

Tests split into `<name>.Test.Unit` (pipeline-step contracts, pure xUnit;
NSubstitute only at the Sender's `IFileAdapter` seam) and
`<name>.Test.Integration` (receive side, send pipeline, composition) built on
the `Intropy.Framework.Testing` fakes: `InMemoryFileAdapter` at both keyed
adapter seams, `FakeEnqueueStep` registered as the receive side's broker edge,
the two platform-service clients swapped the same way (non-empty mode), and a
single NSubstitute stub for the topic subscription when the receive-side tests
run the component's job. Everything is resolved from the real DI graph — built
exactly as production composition does — with only the edges faked. No
sidecar, no Testcontainers.

Note on versions: every `Intropy.Framework.*` package — including
`Intropy.Framework.Testing` — pins at `2.1.0-beta.15`, so the integration fakes
and the framework types they build on always come from the same build.

Components do not run standalone: the job runs via its system host, which
provides every Dapr component (storage bindings, pub/sub, platform services —
including the Intropy Idempotency Service and Business Incident Service the
send pipeline wires in, in non-empty mode).

The template declares `intropy.io/block-kind: transactional-integration`, so
`intropy sys create` assembles it into the system host as a
port-to-port block with no system message. The scaffold record
(`.intropy/scaffold.json`) carries the derived wiring values the host needs:
`fromPort`/`toPort` (the two ports, `<app-id>-source` /
`<app-id>-destination`; the Dapr binding names are the same port names) and
`appId`/`projectName`. The
internal queue between the receive and send pipelines is
component-owned: the topology mints it as the topic `internal-<app-id>` on the
system's pub/sub, `<system>-pubsub`, and nothing declares it. The
host and the deployment pass the pub/sub's name in `INTROPY_PUBSUB_NAME` and
the topic in `INTROPY_TOPIC_NAME`; the framework derives neither. The topic is
unique per component, so two transactional integrations — in one system or in
several sharing a broker — never receive each other's files.

## Container image

The Dockerfile builds with the system folder as its context
(`docker build -f <app-id>/Dockerfile .`), so it copies any
`Directory.Build.props` the system keeps next to its components.
`Dockerfile.dockerignore` limits the context to that file and the components'
`src/` folders. The component folder defaults to the app id; pass
`--build-arg COMPONENT=<folder>` when it differs.

| Name           | Required | Description                                                                                    |
| -------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`         | yes      | PascalCase project/namespace/assembly name (dots allowed, e.g. `Int1055.OrderSync`).           |

| `empty`        | no       | Strip sample step bodies and the idempotency/business-incident wiring for a migration agent to fill in. |

intropy int create transactional -o /tmp/transactional-out \

Yes, one CLI change is needed, and the transactional template needs work before it matters. There is also a deploy gap that affects the extractor too.

**The framework already supports it.** In `intropy-framework`, the transactional receive side's `Sources.Port(SourcePort)` accepts a `PolledSourcePort`. That is how `AddSqlSourcePort` declares the SQL source, so a transactional integration can sweep SQL as it is. The missing pieces are in the templates and the CLI.

**1. CLI: transactional ports can't be external (needs a change)**

The `portKind` support in HEAD (a0fba0fe) only covers single-port blocks:
- `parseTransactional` in `internal/system/blocks.go:173` reads `fromPort` and `toPort` but never a kind.
- `Assemble` (`internal/system/assemble.go:146`) and `mergeWiring` (`internal/system/update.go:531`) only set `Port.Kind` when `name == c.Port`, and transactional blocks leave `c.Port` empty.

So even if the template recorded a kind, a transactional source would still render as `PortRef.Define` with a `./test/<port>` folder. The fix:
- Have the record carry `fromPortKind` (and `toPortKind`, for when a SQL sink arrives). Absent means binding.
- Replace `Component.PortKind` with a kind per port, lined up with `Ports`.
- Use it in `Assemble` and `mergeWiring`.

The system-host template already handles `kind: external` for any port in `Ports.cs`, the development definition and the Taskfile seeding, so it needs no change.

**2. Transactional template: no SQL source yet (in intropy-templates)**

The template only has a file source. It needs the same changes the extractor got in 6bc4ea6:
- a `source: file|sql` parameter
- a `fromPortKind` value
- a `cursorStore` value
- `src/Sql/Query.sql`
- the `Intropy.Framework.Adapters.Sql` package reference
- in `Composition`, `AddSqlSource` and `sources.Port(new PolledSourcePort(...))` replacing the file adapter for the source port
- SQL versions of the receive-side tests

That fits your rule that language knowledge stays in the templates.

**3. Deploy: external ports aren't handled (affects the extractor too)**

`topology.Port` has no kind field. `resolvePortBindingChoices` (`internal/deploy/ports.go:52`) asks for a `--binding` for every port, and neither `deploy-component` nor `deploy-host` mentions external ports or a cursor state store. So `intropy deploy` will probably ask for a file binding for the SQL port and won't create the `<app-id>-cursors` store. I didn't check whether `Intropy.Topology` 2.3.0's graph output includes the port kind or the cursor store. That decides whether the CLI can read them from the topology or has to take them from the scaffold record. If you've only run SQL polling under the local host so far, it's worth trying a deploy.

I've finished the CLI change: `sys create` and `sys update` now mark either port of a transactional integration as external. The full `go test ./...` suite passes. Nothing is committed, because the branch already had uncommitted work (the `--force` confirm and `LockWait`), and I left that as it was.

**What changed**
- **New record keys** (`internal/template/wiring.go`): `fromPortKind` and `toPortKind`. They take `binding` or `external`, the same values as `portKind`, and an absent key means binding.
- **Reading the record** (`internal/system/blocks.go`): a shared `readPortKind` helper now reads `portKind` for extractors and loaders, and `fromPortKind`/`toPortKind` for transactional blocks. Any other value is refused with an error that names the key.
- **Model** (`internal/system/model.go`): `Component.PortKind` is now `PortKinds`, a map from port name to kind with an entry only for external ports. Each port gets its own kind, so `Assemble` and `mergeWiring` no longer check whether it is the block's single port. In the `--output-json` result the field is now `portKinds`. That field was only added this morning in a0fba0fe, so nothing reads it yet.
- **Tests**: `Assemble` gives an external source port its kind while the destination stays a binding; an unknown `toPortKind` is refused; `sys update` stores the two ports with different kinds.
- **README**: documents `portKind` (which a0fba0fe hadn't) and the two new keys.

No system-host template change is needed, since it already handles `kind: external` on any port.

**Still to do before this works end to end**
1. **Transactional template** (intropy-templates): add the `source` parameter, a `fromPortKind` value (`external` when the source is `sql`), a `cursorStore` value, `Query.sql`, the SQL adapter package, and in `Composition`, `AddSqlSource` plus `sources.Port(new PolledSourcePort(...))`, along with SQL receive-side tests.
2. **Deploy** (affects the extractor too): `intropy deploy` will probably still ask for a file binding for an external port, and nothing creates the cursor state store. I haven't checked this.
